info.bio:
Paul Simon nació en Newark (New Jersey) el 13 de octubre de 1941.

A los 9 años coincidió en la escuela con Art Garfunkel, con el que formaría uno de los dúos musicales más importantes de la historia. En 1957 graban un sencillo, con el nombre de Tom y Jerry (Paul Simon era Jerry), titulado "Hey, Schoolgirl!" y consiguieron colocarse entre los 100 primeros de la lista Billboard. Pero no lograron reeditar este éxito y el dúo se deshizo.

Paul Simon prosigue su carrera más adelante en solitario bajo el seudónimo de Jerry Landis.

scenes.name: Les Cousins y el nuevo folk británico
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El revival folk de finales de los cincuenta lo habían moldeado comunistas como Ewan MacColl y Bert Lloyd, para quienes el folk era escritura sagrada de la clase obrera. La nueva generación, nacida durante o justo después de la guerra, vivía la vida: viajaba, okupaba y tocaba en una red de clubes pequeños. Su figura de transición fue Davy Graham, cuya «Angi» (1962) se volvió el estándar de los guitarristas acústicos y que introdujo la afinación DADGAD para imitar el oud que oyó en Marruecos. Les Cousins, abierto en Greek Street el 16 de abril de 1965 como club de toda la noche, fue refugio de fugados y adolescentes de suburbio y semillero de Bert Jansch, Paul Simon, Jackson C. Frank, Roy Harper, Donovan, Sandy Denny, Mick Softley y Anne Briggs: romanticismo maldito, sin temas tabú (prostitución masculina, heroína, salud mental). La trabajadora social Judith Piepe acogía en su piso de Cable Street a Simon, Al Stewart, Denny y Frank.

scenes.name: World beat y funk de la bahía
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: A mediados de los ochenta la bahía de San Francisco vivió un movimiento de baile internacional unido a la lucha contra el apartheid y al apoyo a Centroamérica: ritmistas africanos y caribeños con cantantes, activistas y raperos (Zulu Spear, Big City, Mapenzi, The Looters), en la estela de King Sunny Adé, Fela Kuti y Graceland. Murió antes de cruzar al pop. The Looters (Flashpoint, entre los Clash y EWF) y sobre todo los Freaky Executives, la banda funk orgánica de la zona (premio Bammie 1986, la pulcritud de The Time con los puentes de Tower of Power), desmontada por sus mánagers para encajar en el formato «negro». Toda ciudad tiene sus Freaky Executives. Luego Timex Social Club («Rumors»), Tony! Toni! Toné! («Little Walter», «Feels Good») y los productores Foster & McElroy (Club Nouveau, En Vogue).

scenes.name: Contracultura: cantautores eléctricos
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La fusión de música y política convierte el rock en vehículo de la disidencia: la contracultura. Todo empieza con Bob Dylan, el músico más influyente de los sesenta, que redefine el rock como composición metafísica y libre (Highway 61 Revisited, Blonde On Blonde). La transición del folk-singer al cantautor eléctrico abre infinitas vías: Fred Neil, Tim Hardin, Neil Diamond, Paul Simon (el poeta del chico tímido y solitario), Donovan (la quintaesencia del ideal hippy) y Country Joe McDonald, agit-prop de Berkeley.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los ochenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Absorbida la new wave, el mundo de los cantautores no vuelve a ser el mismo: los referentes pasan a ser Dylan, Neil Young, Cohen, Tim Buckley y Joni Mitchell. Las mujeres recuperan su estatus de seres filosóficos: Phranc, Suzanne Vega, Tracy Chapman, Melissa Etheridge, Michelle Shocked, Barbara Manning, Lucinda y Victoria Williams, Indigo Girls y, en Canadá, Jane Siberry, Mary Margaret O'Hara y Sarah McLachlan. Excéntricos: Jandek, Daniel Johnston, David Thomas, Alejandro Escovedo; en California, Stan Ridgway, Chris Isaak y Smog. En Gran Bretaña, Billy Bragg, Robyn Hitchcock, Julian Cope y, la voz más importante de la década, Nick Cave, predicador del apocalipsis moral (From Her To Eternity, The Good Son). Sinéad O'Connor, Sting, Morrissey, Momus; el pop celta de Enya y Loreena McKennitt; al cambiar la década, Joe Henry, Daniel Lanois y Bob Mould.

podcast.title: "Gamble" Songwriting (1972)
podcast.body: In a 1972 interview with Rolling Stone, Paul Simon characterized "Mother and Child Reunion" as a "gamble," explaining that it represented a style of music he felt unable to create during his partnership with Art Garfunkel. "Simon told John Landau in an interview for Rolling Stone in 1972 that Mother and Child Reunion was the type of song that he could not do when he was teamed up with Art Garfunkel and he considered the song a quote gamble."

podcast.title: Early Career as Jerry Landis
podcast.body: Paul Simon initially performed under the name Jerry Landis as part of the duo Tom and Jerry, who had a minor hit with "Hey School Girl." He later used other aliases like True Taylor and Paul Kane before working under his real name with Art Garfunkel. "Jerry Landis went on to record under other names, like True Taylor and Paul Kane, before getting back together with Tom and deciding to work together under their real names."

podcast.title: Early Collaboration with Carole King
podcast.body: Jerry Landis met Carole King while in college. They recorded demos for other writers together, although they never co-wrote songs. For some of these demos, they reused the name "The Co-Sounds." "Landis and King started working together, recording demos for other writers, they're never writing together."

podcast.title: Jamaican Recording Approach
podcast.body: To achieve an authentic sound, Paul Simon traveled to Jamaica for recordings, where he innovatively compensated session musicians by suggesting they were playing three songs instead of one, effectively providing them more money than the standard "notorious racket" of about seven dollars per song with no royalties, and crucially, he allowed them to freely play "whatever they want." "So I sat down and said you play it, play what you want. That's the key thing. Let them play whatever they want and then you change, you go their way."

podcast.title: Legal Trademark Requirement
podcast.body: Paul Simon was legally obligated by Kodak to include specific fine print on his records for "Kodachrome," indicating that "Kodachrome" was a registered trademark of the company. This showcased the intersection of copyright law and corporate branding in the music industry. "Paul Simon was legally compelled by Codac to include fine print on his records indicating that Codacrome was a registered trademark of the company."

podcast.body: Paul Simon was cited as an example of artists popular in the early 1970s whose music contributed to the "Mellow" trend, as fans deserted the harder, more soulful sounds of the 60s for a softer approach. "The word everyone was using was Mellow, James Taylor, Bread, Olivia Newton John, Paul Simon, the California Rock of the Eagles, a new look Fleetwood Mac."

podcast.title: Multiple Aliases and Real Identity
podcast.body: After his brief collaboration with Carole King, Jerry Landis recorded under other names, including True Taylor and Paul Kane. He eventually reunited with his partner "Tom" and decided to work under their real names, revealing Jerry Landis to be Paul Simon, and "Tom" to be Art Garfunkel. "They didn't work together for very long, and Jerry Landis went on to record under other names, like True Taylor and Paul Kane, before getting back together with Tom and deciding to work together under their real names."

podcast.title: Repeat Grammy Winner Discussion
podcast.body: Paul Simon's multiple Grammy wins, including one with Simon and Garfunkel and later for "Graceland," were used to illustrate the debate around repeat winners. It was suggested that not giving him a repeat Grammy in 1976 might have opened a path for Elton John's "Captain Fantastic and the Brown Dirt Cowboy" to win Album of the Year. "Not giving Paul Simon a repeat Grammy in 1976. Remember, he'd already won with Simon and Garfunkel and would win again a decade later for Graceland."

podcast.body: Don Kirshner and Al Nevins, owners of Aldon Music, signed Paul Simon as a talented new songwriter around the same time they signed Neil Sedaka, Howard Greenfield, Barry Mann, and Cynthia Weil. xref.title: Musical Development and Hard Rock Focus
xref.body: By 1967, Nancy and Ann were performing as The Viewpoints, with Nancy also doing solo shows influenced by Joni Mitchell and Paul Simon, as well as rock figures like John Lennon, Paul McCartney, Jimi Hendrix, and Jimmy Page. As their groups evolved into Heart, Nancy increasingly focused on hard rock and discovered drop D tuning, a technique that would become vital to the grunge era 15 years later. "By the time some of the various groups she was in with Ann evolved into Hart, Nancy had become much more focused on hard rock and she discovered drop D tuning, something that would become essential to the grunge era 15 years later."
